data:
The redfish command ships with the module since v0.3.0. It is a cobra command tree with POSIX flags and --help on every command. Results go to standard output and errors to standard error. This page follows the --help of v0.8.0.
go install github.com/go-redfish/redfish/cmd/redfish@v0.8.0
data.accounts#accounts:
Since v0.7.0, redfish accounts drives the AccountService: the Accounts commands of redfish_command and the ListUsers and GetAccountServiceConfig commands of redfish_info. An account is named by its user name, or by --id (its Id).
Command What it does accounts list the accounts, without the empty slots (ListUsers) accounts add USERNAME creates the account; nothing is done when the user exists (AddUser) accounts delete USERNAME deletes the account; nothing is done when it does not exist (DeleteUser) accounts enable, disable EnableUser, DisableUser accounts password sets the account’s password (UpdateUserPassword) accounts rename UpdateUserName accounts role sets RoleId (UpdateUserRole) accounts types sets AccountTypes and/or OEMAccountTypes accounts roles the roles of the service accounts config [set] shows the AccountService (GetAccountServiceConfig) or changes it A new password comes only from --new-password-file (mode 0600) or --new-password-stdin. No flag takes it and no environment variable is read. It is never printed, and an error from a service that echoes it back is redacted. Some services have a fixed number of account slots and refuse POST and DELETE. On those, like the Ansible modules, add fills an empty slot (or the one --id names) with a PATCH and delete empties the account.
data.chassis#chassis:
Since v0.5.0, redfish chassis reads and drives the Chassis resources: the Chassis commands of the Ansible modules redfish_command and redfish_info. --id names one chassis (the last segment of its path). Like the Ansible modules, the reading commands (inventory, fans, power, thermals, psu, health, hpe) cover every chassis when no --id is given. The other commands act on one chassis: the only one, or the one --id names. Without --id, a service with several chassis gets an error that lists them.
Command What it reads or does chassis list lists the chassis (their paths) chassis inventory the identity of the chassis (GetChassisInventory) chassis power PowerControl of the Power resources (GetChassisPower) chassis thermals temperatures of the Thermal resources (GetChassisThermals) chassis fans fans of the Thermal resources (GetFanInventory) chassis psu power supplies present (GetPsuInventory) chassis health the health of the chassis, its power supplies, fans and PCIe devices (GetHealthReport) chassis led the indicator LED: on, off, blink chassis sensors the Sensor resources (Sensors collection) chassis power-subsystem PowerSubsystem and its power supplies chassis thermal-subsystem ThermalSubsystem, its fans and ThermalMetrics chassis metrics EnvironmentMetrics: power, energy, temperature, fan speeds chassis hpe HPE OEM settings covered by the Ansible modules: thermal-config, fan-percent-min The Power and Thermal resources are deprecated in favour of PowerSubsystem, ThermalSubsystem and Sensors, but many BMCs still serve only them, so the command reads both.
data.example#Example: redfish mock serve --ca-out ./mock-ca.pem & # prints https://127.0.0.1:PORT printf 'password' > pw && chmod 600 pw E=--endpoint=https://127.0.0.1:PORT redfish $E --ca-file ./mock-ca.pem --user admin --password-file pw session login redfish $E --ca-file ./mock-ca.pem --session raw get /redfish/v1/Systems redfish $E --ca-file ./mock-ca.pem --session systems power PowerForceOff redfish $E --ca-file ./mock-ca.pem --session session logout
data.global#Global flags: Flag Meaning --endpoint the BMC’s address, https://host[:port] --user user name --password-file file holding the password (mode 0600) --session use the session saved by redfish session login instead of the password --ca-file PEM file of the CAs that sign the BMC’s certificate (default: the system roots) --insecure do not verify the BMC’s certificate; prints a warning on stderr and cannot be combined with --ca-file --timeout per-request timeout (default 10s) -o, --output json (default) or table There is no password flag and no password environment variable. The password is read from a file, so it never appears in a process listing or a shell history.
data.managers#managers:
Since v0.6.0, redfish managers drives the Manager resources (the BMC itself): the Manager commands of the three Ansible modules. inventory, health and nic get cover every manager when no --id is given. The other commands act on one manager: the only one, or the one --id names.
Command What it reads or does managers list lists the managers (their paths) managers inventory identity and firmware (GetManagerInventory) managers health the health of the managers managers power PowerGracefulRestart (alias GracefulRestart), PowerOn, PowerForceOff, PowerForceRestart, PowerGracefulShutdown, PowerReboot; --wait blocks until the service answers again (--wait-delay, --wait-timeout) managers reset-to-defaults ResetAll, PreserveNetworkAndUsers, PreserveNetwork managers network-protocols the network services (HTTP, SSH, IPMI…): get, set managers ntp set the NTP service managers datetime the date, time and UTC offset: get, set managers nic the manager’s network interfaces: get, set managers host-interface the host interfaces: get, set managers service-id ServiceIdentification: get, set managers logs the entries of the log services, and logs clear managers virtual-media get, insert, eject managers virtual-media insert --image URL puts the image in the first free slot that supports one of the --media-type values. It uses the InsertMedia action when the slot has one, else a PATCH. Nothing is sent when the image is already inserted. The password to fetch the image is read from --image-password-file (mode 0600), never given on the command line.
v0.6.0 also added systems virtual-media (get, insert, eject) for services that attach virtual media to the system, systems logs (entries and clear) and chassis logs.
data.mock#mock serve:
redfish mock serve starts the mock BMC over HTTPS. It uses a self-signed certificate valid for 24 hours, writes that certificate to --ca-out (pass it back as --ca-file), prints the endpoint and stops on interrupt.
Flag Meaning --listen address to listen on (default 127.0.0.1:0, a free loopback port) --ca-out where to write the certificate (default: under the user config directory) --mock-password-file file holding admin’s password; without it the password is password --task-polls how many times a task monitor answers 202 before the task completes (default 2)
data.next#Coming next: Commands for the last area (storage) come one minor release at a time, and each is marked in Parity as it lands.
data.raw#raw:
redfish raw sends one request to a path of the service (/redfish/...) and prints the body.
Command Request raw get PATH GET a resource raw head PATH HEAD: status and headers (ETag) raw patch PATH --data … [--if-match ETAG] PATCH properties; a stale --if-match is answered 412 raw put PATH --data … PUT: replace a resource raw post PATH --data … POST: create a member or invoke an action raw delete PATH DELETE a resource --data is the JSON body: the text itself, @file, or - for standard input. A 202 answer names a task monitor: the monitor is printed on stderr and the Task body on stdout. A non-2xx answer is an error that carries what the service said: its code, its message and @Message.ExtendedInfo.
data.session#session: Command What it does redfish session login logs in with --user and --password-file by POSTing to the Sessions collection (DSP0266 13.3.4). The X-Auth-Token is saved in a 0600 file under the user’s config directory and is never printed redfish session status says whether a session is saved for --endpoint redfish session logout ends the saved session at the BMC and removes its file redfish session list lists the active sessions of the service (v0.7.0) redfish session clear ends every active session of the service, its own last (v0.7.0) redfish session config changes SessionService properties (v0.7.0) Afterwards, pass --session to any command instead of --user and --password-file.
data.systems#systems:
Since v0.4.0, redfish systems drives the ComputerSystem resources: the Systems commands of the Ansible modules redfish_command, redfish_config and redfish_info. When the service has several systems, --id names the one to use (the last segment of its path). Without --id, such a service gets an error that lists the systems.
Command What it does systems list lists the systems (their paths) systems power PowerOn, PowerForceOff, PowerForceRestart, PowerGracefulRestart, PowerGracefulShutdown, PowerReboot, PowerCycle, PowerFullPowerCycle, each checked against the ResetType values the service allows systems boot-override the boot source override: get, set, disable systems boot-order the boot order: get, set, default systems bios BIOS attributes: get, set (through @Redfish.Settings), verify, reset, registry systems secure-boot UEFI Secure Boot: enable, disable systems power-restore-policy get, set systems led the system’s indicator LED: on, off, blink systems asset-tag sets AssetTag systems inventory system, cpu, memory, nic, psu systems health the health of the system and its subsystems systems logs the entries of the system’s log services, and logs clear (v0.6.0) systems virtual-media get, insert, eject (v0.6.0) Each command’s flags are in its --help.
data.update#update:
Since v0.8.0, redfish update drives the UpdateService: the Update commands of redfish_command and redfish_info.
Command What it does update simple asks the BMC to fetch an image and update with it (SimpleUpdate) update push uploads an image to the MultipartHttpPushUri, streamed from the file (MultipartHTTPPushUpdate) update status the status of an update: its task or job (GetUpdateStatus) update operations performs what the update asks for to continue: its resets (PerformRequestedOperations) update inventory [--software] the firmware inventory, or the software inventory update capabilities what the service can do: multipart push, actions, transfer protocols simple and push start a task. Its monitor is printed on stderr and not awaited, like redfishtool’s -N. Add --watch to follow the task to its end; progress goes to stderr. push accepts only a regular file and refuses one larger than --max-size (4 GiB by default) before it sends anything. The image is streamed, never loaded whole into memory. The image server’s password comes from --image-password-file (mode 0600) or --image-password-stdin. A password written inside the image URI is refused.

data.errors#Errors: A refused URL is an ErrInsecure. An HTTP status the BMC answered is a *StatusError, which carries the Redfish error’s code, message and extended info. Both can be tested with errors.Is and errors.As.
data.install#Install: go get github.com/go-redfish/redfish@v0.8.0 The library has no dependency outside the standard library. The redfish command, in cmd/redfish, also uses cobra.
data.meter#Turn reads into energy:
A Meter turns the successive readings of one BMC into intervals:
var m redfish.Meter // MaxGap 0 means 5 minutes for range time.Tick(time.Minute) { r, err := c.Read(ctx) if err != nil { continue } iv, ok := m.Observe(r) if !ok { continue // the first read is only a baseline } if !iv.Valid { fmt.Println("no energy:", iv.Reason) // never bill 0 as a measurement continue } fmt.Printf("%s %.4f kWh\n", iv.Source, iv.KWh) } With a counter the interval is the counter’s difference, exact even if reads were missed. With only a power it is the trapezoid of two samples, an estimate between them, and samples further apart than MaxGap are not joined. A counter that goes down (a reboot) gives an invalid interval with the reason counter reset, never a negative energy.
data.read#Read a node:
A Client reads one BMC. The address must be https and must carry no credentials; the credentials are given apart, through Credentials, so a password lives as long as a request.
package main import ( "context" "fmt" "log" "time" "github.com/go-redfish/redfish" ) func main() { c, err := redfish.New(redfish.Config{ BaseURL: "https://bmc.example.org", Credentials: redfish.Static{User: "monitor", Password: readSecret()}, Session: true, // log in once, send X-Auth-Token, log out on Close CAFile: "/etc/ssl/bmc-ca.pem", Timeout: 10 * time.Second, }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } ctx := context.Background() defer c.Close(ctx) r, err := c.Read(ctx) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } switch { case r.EnergyKWh != nil: fmt.Printf("%s: %.3f kWh (counter)\n", r.Chassis, *r.EnergyKWh) case r.PowerWatts != nil: fmt.Printf("%s: %.0f W\n", r.Chassis, *r.PowerWatts) } } (readSecret is yours: read the password from a file or a secret store, never from a command line or an environment variable.)
Read takes the EnergykWh counter of the chassis’ EnvironmentMetrics; with no counter, its power (PowerWatts, else the PowerControl of the Power resource). The service is discovered once, from /redfish/v1, and the links it gives are remembered. Config.MetricsPath skips discovery when you know the resource; Config.Chassis picks one chassis out of several.
data.requests#Any other request:
The generic methods reach any resource of the service:
r, err := c.Get(ctx, "/redfish/v1/Systems/437XR1138R2") // change a property only if nobody changed the resource since it was read _, err = c.Patch(ctx, "/redfish/v1/Systems/437XR1138R2", map[string]any{"AssetTag": "rack-12"}, r.ETag()) Post invokes an action. When the service answers 202 with a task monitor, WaitTask polls the monitor until the task ends. Do takes a full Request when you need another method or header. To try any of these without a real machine, see the mock BMC.
data.systems#Systems: Since v0.4.0 the client drives the ComputerSystem resources the way the Ansible modules do: SystemPower and ManagePower, SetBootOverride and SetBootOrder, BiosAttributes, SetBiosAttributes and VerifyBiosAttributes, SetSecureBoot, SetPowerRestorePolicy, SetIndicatorLED, SetAssetTag, the inventories (SystemInventory, CPUInventory, MemoryInventory, NICInventory, PSUInventory) and SystemHealthReport. Like the Ansible modules, a power command is mapped to a ResetType the service allows (its ActionInfo or AllowableValues). Nothing is sent when the system is already in the state asked for, and an action the resource does not have is ErrUnsupported. With several systems, ResolveSystem picks one by id. Without an id, such a service returns ErrAmbiguous. The systems commands call these functions.

data.behaviour#How it behaves:
Each rule comes from DSP0266 1.23.0:
the service root and /redfish are open. Every other request needs HTTP Basic or an X-Auth-Token (13.3), else it gets 401 with a Redfish error; a POST to SessionService/Sessions logs in (13.3.4.2) and answers 201 with a Location naming the Session and an X-Auth-Token header. A DELETE of the Session logs out; every resource has an ETag. A PATCH whose If-Match does not match gets 412 (6.5, 7.6); a PATCH merges the properties sent into the resource and answers with the result; a POST to a collection creates a member (201 and Location) and a DELETE removes it; a POST to an action target is checked against the AllowableValues of its parameters. ComputerSystem.Reset changes PowerState; UpdateService.SimpleUpdate answers 202 with a task monitor in Location and a Retry-After header (12.2). The monitor answers 202 TaskPolls times, then 200 with the Task; an error is the Redfish error object with @Message.ExtendedInfo (8.6, 9.5.11). State is kept in memory. BMC.Log() returns every request served (METHOD path status) and BMC.Resource(path) returns a resource’s current JSON, both for assertions.
b, _ := mockbmc.New(mockbmc.Options{}) // admin / password srv := httptest.NewTLSServer(b.Handler()) defer srv.Close() // point redfish.Config.BaseURL at srv.URL and trust srv.Certificate()
data.not#What it is not: It does not model any vendor’s firmware. A client that passes against it follows the DMTF documents, which does not prove that it works on your hardware. Faults such as a counter reset, a gap in power samples or an oversized, malformed, slow or redirecting answer are not built into the mock. The client’s own tests inject them with dedicated httptest servers.
data.serves#What it serves: The tree is the DMTF public-rackmount1 mockup (DSP2043, BSD-3-Clause), vendored with its licence. It has one system (437XR1138R2), one chassis (1U) and one manager (BMC), with the account, session, event, update, task, certificate and key services, BIOS, secure boot, virtual media, log services, sensors, EnvironmentMetrics, and both the older Power/Thermal resources and the newer PowerSubsystem/ThermalSubsystem.
data.trees#Two trees:
A client tuned to one tree learns that tree’s shortcuts, so since v0.4.0 the mock can serve a second one: mockbmc.Options{Tree: mockbmc.TreeEmulator} serves emulator-1u, the static tree of the DMTF Redfish Interface Emulator (BSD-3-Clause). That tree has no Links.Sessions, and its collections link their members differently. The default is mockbmc.TreeRackmount. The library’s Systems tests run against both trees. redfish mock serve always serves the rackmount tree.
For BIOS settings, boot order and action checks, the mock adds what the static trees lack: a BootOrder, @Redfish.ActionInfo resources, a BIOS attribute registry and BIOS Settings applied immediately.
data.why#Why a mock: A test suite should never talk to a real machine: a BMC can power a server off, and nobody runs a suite that needs one. The package mockbmc (since v0.3.0) is a Redfish service that a test starts in-process. A developer can also start it from the command line with redfish mock serve.

data.method#How parity is judged: The reference is the oracle: a behaviour is ported exactly, then compared with the reference’s answer on the same input, and a difference is either a defect to fix or a documented, deliberate departure. The departures worth knowing already: the client refuses a non-https address and an HTTP redirect, on purpose, whatever the reference accepts.
data.status#Where it stands:
The authoritative table is PARITY.md in the redfish repository, committed with the code it describes, so that a command is marked done in the same change that implements it. This page does not copy it, because a copy is what drifts.
What exists in v0.8.0:
Capability In v0.8.0 service root and discovery yes Basic and session authentication yes energy counter and power reading yes energy from reads (Meter) yes generic requests (Do, Get, Patch with If-Match, Post, Delete, WaitTask) yes mock BMC yes redfish command: sessions, raw requests, systems, chassis, managers, accounts, mock yes Systems commands of the three modules yes (v0.4.0; virtual media in v0.6.0), except storage (with Storage) Chassis commands of the two modules yes (v0.5.0) Manager commands of the three modules yes (v0.6.0) Accounts and Sessions commands yes (v0.7.0) Update commands yes (v0.8.0) storage (v0.9.0) to come At v0.8.0, 94 of the 99 commands are done. The 5 others are the storage commands.
Any of the 99 commands can already be sent by hand with redfish raw. A dedicated command adds what the Ansible module adds on top of the request: discovery of the right resource, a check of the allowed values and waiting for the task.
data.target#The target: The behaviour of the Ansible modules community.general.redfish_info, redfish_command and redfish_config, which are themselves built on the Redfish Specification and the DMTF redfishtool. A Go program that needs a BMC’s answers should not have to shell out to a Python client to get them.

data: A BMC is a privileged network service, often old and rarely patched, and it holds the keys to the machine. The client therefore treats what it says as data to check, and what it is given as secrets to keep short-lived. Every rule below is in github.com/go-redfish/redfish at v0.8.0; the package documentation cites the DMTF text it comes from.
data.bounds#What the client bounds: Size. An answer is read up to MaxBody (1 MiB); a larger one is ErrTooLarge, never an allocation of the size the server announces. Time. Config.Timeout bounds every request, and the contexts you pass cancel them. Shape. A reply that is not the JSON the schema describes is ErrMalformed. Readings that are negative, not finite or absurdly large are discarded by the decoders rather than passed on.
data.command#The command:
The redfish command follows the same rules, with these additions:
there is no password flag and no password environment variable. The password is read from --password-file, whose mode should be 0600; session login saves the session token in a 0600 file under the user’s config directory and never prints it. session logout ends the session at the BMC and removes the file; a password the command sends to the BMC (a new account’s password, an image server’s password) is read only from a 0600 file or standard input. In the library, an account password is a Secret, which prints as [redacted] in every format, and an error from a service that echoes it back is redacted (v0.7.0). The same holds for an image server’s password since v0.8.0, and a password written inside an image URI is refused; update push streams the image from a regular file and refuses one larger than --max-size before it sends anything (v0.8.0); --insecure turns certificate verification off for one run. You have to ask for it explicitly, it prints a warning on stderr, and it is refused together with --ca-file.
data.fuzzing#Fuzzing and CI: The two JSON decoders (ParseEnvironmentMetrics, ParsePowerConsumed) and the meter are fuzzed, and the inputs that once found a defect are committed under testdata/fuzz/. CI runs go vet, go test -race, a short fuzz run and govulncheck on every change.
data.limits#What it does not do: It does not pin a certificate by fingerprint, only by authority. It does not rate-limit: a caller that polls a BMC every second may exhaust the BMC, which is itself a small computer. A minute is a sensible interval for energy.
data.mock#The mock BMC: The mock BMC is a test double. Its default password is password, it keeps everything in memory, and redfish mock serve listens on loopback by default with a self-signed certificate that is valid for 24 hours. Do not expose it on a network.
data.refuses#What the client refuses: Refused Because Error a URL whose scheme is not https a password travels with every request (Redfish Specification: Basic authentication requires HTTPS) ErrInsecure credentials in the URL a URL ends up in logs, history and error messages ErrInsecure a query or a fragment in the base URL the base is an address, not a request ErrInsecure a MetricsPath outside /redfish/ a configured path must stay inside the service ErrInsecure an HTTP redirect a BMC that sends the client elsewhere would be sent the credentials there the redirect response is returned as an error turning certificate verification off Config has no such setting; a caller that passes its own Config.HTTP client is responsible for that client’s TLS settings none Certificates are verified against the system roots or, with Config.CAFile, against the authorities in that PEM file (a BMC usually has a private one). TLS 1.2 is the floor.
data.secrets#Secrets:
Credentials is asked for the user and the password when a request needs them, so the caller resolves its secret reference at that moment and the library keeps nothing longer. Error messages are scrubbed of the secrets they could carry. With Config.Session, the password is sent once, to the SessionService; the token is then used, and Close logs the session out.
Keep the password out of command lines and environment variables, where every process of the machine can read it: read it from a file whose mode you check.
